**Verdict: conditional GO** for the one discarded queue179032 mechanics17 unit. The four fresh100 units (control032, candidate032, candidate041, control041) stay gated on that unit passing, with no changes. I don't recommend a kill. This was a read-only review: I edited no repo files and ran no Torch or GPU work. I did save a memory note outside the repo. ## Blocker (one, and your working-tree edit already contains the fix) **1. Requiring the receipt RSS to equal the log RSS is an invalid rule.** - The receipt reads `getrusage` before it writes the receipt and before Python shuts down, so it can only be a lower bound. `/usr/bin/time` reports the peak over the whole process lifetime. - Startup shows the gap: 960,024 KiB in the receipt versus 998,348 KiB in the log. - If the rule stays, the mechanics phase rejects the startup log. Even if it didn't, the train phase would later reject the mechanics log, so the fresh100 units could never start after you had spent a GPU run on mechanics. - The fix at `train_image_queue_adaptation.py:55`, `0 < snapshot ≤ int(rss[0]) ≤ 8 GiB`, is the right minimal authority for the whole unit: - **Time:** the systemd `Service runtime` line, capped. - **Memory:** the final RSS from the inner `/usr/bin/time`, capped at 8 GiB. The in-process `memory.max`=8G, `swap.max`=0 and cgroup-membership checks, plus `Memory swap peak: 0B`, confirm the configuration. - **Identity:** the invocation ID in the `Running as unit` line, plus the sha256 of each file. RSS equality never bound identity, so relaxing it lets in no foreign receipt or log. - Taking the first RSS match by position still fails safely: if the inner timer were missing, `rss[0]` would be systemd-run's ~7 MB, which is below any real snapshot. - Don't use systemd's `Memory peak` for anything. It reads 256K–1M for processes using 3.6–8.6 GB in about 15 historical logs. **Consequence you can't skip:** the edited driver (`c88df6…`) no longer matches the frozen driver (`6c72c1…`) in manifest `7324ba…`. Before mechanics you need to: - freeze a new train manifest with the new driver and test hashes; - stage a new unchanging source root; - rerun startup (about 13 s, CPU only); - keep startup-v1 as history only. The CPU118 proof (`5d4909…`) stays valid, because that closure's 118 files are unchanged. `startup["execution_sha256"] == args.execution_sha256` will correctly reject startup-v1 under the new manifest. ## Checks that hold as written - **Sampler:** it keeps the original class slots exactly and uses SHA256-ordered cycles. It raises an error on bad classes, rows or seeds and uses no RNG. The 6330/6331 unique-image counts and the class-sequence hash are rechecked at runtime for both arms. - **Resume:** the sampler state is fully determined by the step number plus the schedule hash for that arm. The resume identity includes the schedule, class sequence and `sampling_arm`. `validate_resume` requires the whole identity to match, so a control checkpoint can't resume a queue run. - **Full-state exactness:** 400 vision tensors, head, classifier, bank, buffers, AdamW state, scaler and both RNG states round-trip. Mechanics compares the replayed steps 8+9 and the terminal fingerprint against the uninterrupted 17 steps. The fresh candidate032 run must match mechanics steps 1–17 exactly, image IDs included. - **Augmentation:** it is seeded per step (`SEED*100000+step`), so it carries no hidden state. The initial fingerprint doesn't include RNG, so one CPU initial fingerprint serves both seeds. The rank-active flag is the same in both arms. ## Recommended while you refreeze anyway (not blockers) - In `validate_mechanics`, also assert: - `startup_authority_sha256 == args.startup_sha256` - `cpu_execution_sha256 == args.cpu_execution_sha256` - `resume_identity["schedule_sha256"] == schedule_sha256` - Optionally tie the RSS reading to the timed-command block containing `--phase

… --execution-sha256 ` instead of taking the first match. - Before launch, check free disk and remove any stale `discard-image-queue-*` folders. A kill at `RuntimeMaxSec` would leave about two full checkpoints in the source root. - Leave the legacy `"arm": "half"` field in the identity alone; it's harmless. ## Cost and resource risks (these fail safely; they are not code defects) - **Time:** the historical boundary10 mechanics run took 107.8 s against the 120 s cap. Boundary12 steps take about 1.15 s versus 1.26 s and write smaller checkpoints, so I'd expect about 100–105 s. - **RSS:** that run peaked at 8,133,180 KiB against 8,388,608, which is 97%. The gate now checks the final peak, which is at least the snapshot, so the margin is about 3%. - **Train units:** the boundary12 controls took 151–153 s against the 300 s cap, and their projection sits well under 269 s. No concern. ## Statistical contract It is sound as frozen. It can resolve about ±0.2 pp: - The two historical controls (seeds 032 and 041) disagree on 36 vs 33 held queries, a net of +0.047 pp. That is one sample of seed-to-seed training noise, and it sits well below the +0.20 pp bar. - The late-dense negative came from −12 and −14 net queries per seed. The chance of a gain is low. This is a 20% re-draw of image slots within 100 updates, on a model that has already seen every fit image about 4.8 times. The whole run costs roughly 30–40 minutes, and a negative closes the recipe, so it's still worth running. ## Required before scoring (not needed to admit mechanics) The frozen adapter for held export and scoring must: - accept only `image-queue-train-v1` receipts from `image-queue-adaptation-v1` with the expected arm and seed schedule hashes; - reject late-dense receipts; - check each train unit's own log with the relaxed RSS rule and a 300 s cap, because the driver never checks its own train log; - compute cost ratios only against controls run at the same time.
